prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The sad-eyed man appears alive despite being a static or imagined figure, puffing cigars amid a scene of gillyflowers, an apple, purple bells, and a grassy hill.
- He expresses sadness because he has locked his head in a Japanese box and lost the key, leaving him unable to see the gillyflowers and purple bells beside him.
- When he asks the narrator to look and describe the scene, the narrator confesses their eyes have grown "sugary and dim" from too much reading by candlelight.
- The narrator similarly cannot recall what they've read, as their memory has grown tired from focusing on invisible things, having also locked away and lost the key to their own head.
- Recognizing their shared condition, the sad-eyed man declares they are one and the same, promising to write the narrator into the idyllic scene so they can both puff cigars together "as if alive."

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Sarah, The, Gillyflowers

outputs.L1:
(for Sarah, when she's older)

The round and sad-eyed man puffed his cigar as though he were truly alive. Gillyflowers bloomed to the left of the apple, purple bells hung to the right, and a grass-covered hill rose behind them all.

"I am sad today," said the sad-eyed man, "for I have locked my head inside a Japanese box and lost the key." "I am sad today," he told me, "for there are gillyflowers beside the apple, and purple bells I cannot see. Will you look upon them for me," he asked, "and tell me what you find?"

"I cannot," I replied, "for my eyes have grown sugary and dim from reading too long by candlelight."

"Then tell me what you've read," said the round and sad-eyed man.

"I cannot," I replied, "for my memory has grown weary and dim from gazing at things no light can ever reveal—and I, too, have locked my head in a Japanese box and cast away the key."

"Then I am you, and you are me," said the sad-eyed man, as though he were truly alive. "I shall write you into the place where I belong—between the gillyflowers and the purple bells, the apple and the hill—and together we shall puff our cigars from noon till night, as though we were alive."
outputs.L2:
(dedicated to Sarah, for her future self)

The heavyset gentleman with mournful eyes drew on his cigar smoke as though breath still moved through him. To his left bloomed gillyflowers beside an apple, purple bells rose on his right, and a green slope rolled out behind. "Today sorrow fills me," the melancholy man confessed, "because I've sealed my mind inside a box from Japan and misplaced its key." He continued, "My sadness comes from knowing gillyflowers grow near that apple, and purple bells exist nearby—yet I cannot glimpse them." He inquired whether I might observe these things in his place and report back what I discovered. I told him this was impossible, explaining that my vision had turned cloudy and sweet-tinged from too many nights spent reading beside flickering candles. "Then share with me what you've learned from your reading," he requested. Again I refused, admitting my recollection had grown weary and hazy from staring at things no light could ever illuminate—and besides, I too had trapped my mind within a Japanese box, casting the key aside forever. "Then you have become me, and I have become you," the man declared, his aliveness undiminished. "I shall place you exactly where you belong—nestled among the gillyflowers, the purple bells, the apple, and the hillside—and together we shall smoke our cigars from midday until darkness falls, both of us breathing still."
outputs.L3:
# The Man in the Japanese Box

There is a peculiar vitality to the sad-eyed man, though by all rights he ought to possess none at all. He is, after all, nothing more than a static arrangement—perhaps only imagined, perhaps only remembered—and yet he sits there puffing on his cigar with all the unhurried contentment of someone thoroughly alive. Around him the scene arranges itself with strange precision: gillyflowers nodding in some invisible breeze, a single apple resting nearby, purple bells scattered like fallen notes, and beneath it all, the soft green slope of a grassy hill. It is an idyllic tableau, the kind one might find pressed between the pages of an old book, and yet the man within it seems to breathe.

His sadness, when it surfaces, is peculiar in its origin. He confesses that he has locked his own head inside a Japanese box—some lacquered, intricate thing—and in doing so has misplaced the key. The consequence is absurd and yet somehow tragic: he cannot see the very gillyflowers and purple bells that surround him, cannot turn his gaze to the beauty that his own scene contains. He is a man surrounded by loveliness he can no longer perceive, trapped by his own doing in a darkness of his own construction.

So he turns to the narrator, asking for help—asking simply that they look upon the scene and describe it to him, since he cannot do so himself. But the narrator's confession is no less strange than his own. Their eyes, they admit, have grown "sugary and dim," clouded by too many hours spent reading in the thin, flickering light of candles. The world has softened into a blur; clarity has been traded for the accumulated weight of pages turned in darkness.

And it does not end there. The narrator, pressed further, finds they cannot even recall what it was they read—the very words that dimmed their sight have themselves escaped memory. Their recollection has grown tired, worn thin from the strain of focusing on things that were never truly visible to begin with, things existing only in the mind's eye, invisible as the box's missing key. And in this admission comes the quiet revelation: the narrator, too, has locked away their own head, has lost their own key, has sealed themselves off from the world in a manner not so different from the sad-eyed man's.

It is this recognition—this mirrored affliction—that draws the man's sorrow into something like joy. He declares, with sudden certainty, that they are one and the same: two figures who have each imprisoned their own sight, each forgotten the way back to clarity. And so he makes his promise. He will write the narrator into the scene beside him, into the gillyflowers and the purple bells, onto the grassy hill beneath the watching apple. There they will sit together, two boxed and keyless heads, puffing their cigars in shared and companionable stillness—not truly alive, perhaps, but rendered so convincingly, so gently, that they might as well be. *As if alive.*
outputs.L4:
The hill was the color of old paper, and on it grew gillyflowers in such abundance that their scent became a kind of weather, thick and clove-sweet, pressing against my temples like the beginning of a fever. Purple bells hung among them, ringing without sound, and near my feet lay an apple, whole and untouched, as if someone had set it there deliberately and then forgotten why.

I did not notice the man at first. He was round in the way that certain old moons are round, sitting cross-legged in the flowers with his hands folded over his stomach, and his eyes were the saddest I had ever seen—not sad with grief, but sad the way a closed door is sad, or a song remembered only in fragments.

"You've come to ask about the hill," he said, though I had asked nothing.

"I've come because I woke up here," I told him. "Though I couldn't say from what."

He nodded slowly, as though this confirmed something he'd long suspected. "I understand. I myself cannot see the flowers."

I looked at him, at the gillyflowers pressing against his round shoulders, the purple bells nodding near his ear. "But they're right beside you."

"That doesn't matter. My eyes are elsewhere. I put them away." He said this simply, the way one might mention misplacing a set of keys. "I keep my head in a box. Japanese lacquer, black with a little gold along the seams. I locked it years ago—or minutes ago, I can no longer tell which—and swallowed the key, or buried it, or perhaps only forgot where I'd set it down. In any case, I cannot see the flowers. I only know they're there because you've told me."

Something in his words loosened a stone in my chest. "That's strange," I said, "because I have done the very same thing. My head is in a box too. Also lacquered. Also locked." I touched my own face as I said it, half expecting to find nothing there, only smoothness, only the suggestion of a face rather than the thing itself. "I don't remember why I did it. I only remember the weight of the lid closing."

The sad-eyed man looked at me—or seemed to, though by his own account he could not truly see anything at all. "Then how is it," he asked, "that you can describe the gillyflowers to me? How do you know the bells are purple, or that there's an apple by your foot, if your sight is locked away with the rest of you?"

I had no answer. I looked down at the apple and found that I could no longer remember picking it up, or setting it down, or whether it was mine at all.

"Perhaps," he said slowly, each word arriving like something long stored in a drawer, "we are not two people sitting on a hill. Perhaps there is only the hill, and the flowers, and one man who has locked his head away twice, and forgotten twice, and so believes himself to be in conversation with someone else."

The gillyflowers seemed to lean in closer as he said it, or perhaps it was only that the boundary between us had grown thin enough to let the wind move through both our chests at once. I felt his sadness the way one feels a memory not one's own—suddenly, completely, without the comfort of distance. And I understood, in the way one understands the end of a dream even while still dreaming it, that he was right. There had only ever been the one of us. The box, the flowers, the apple, the hill—all of it had been arranged by a single hand, and that hand had built two mouths only so that the silence might have something to talk to.

"Well," the sad-eyed man said, and here something almost like warmth entered his ruined voice, "if we are the same, then let us at least be good company for ourselves."

He reached into his coat—my coat—and produced two cigars, offering one across the space that had stopped, by then, being a space at all.

"I will write myself into this hill," he told me, striking a match that flared too brightly against the pale afternoon. "Into the gillyflowers, the bells, the apple you can't remember holding. I'll set myself down here permanently, so that some part of us will always be sitting among these flowers, sad-eyed and round and pretending—only pretending—that we are still among the living."

I took the cigar. The smoke rose between us, or between the two folds of the one thing we had become, curling up past the purple bells toward a sky that neither of us, strictly speaking, could see. We smoked without speaking further, two ceremonial gestures performed by a single body split down some invisible seam, and the hill held us the way a locked box holds whatever has been sealed inside it—gently, permanently, and without any further need for explanation.
outputs.L5:
# The Gillyflowers

Sarah had always loved the gillyflowers that grew along the garden wall, their sweet clove-like scent drifting through the open kitchen window each summer evening. Her grandmother had planted them decades ago, and now Sarah tended them with the same quiet devotion.

The flowers came in shades of deep purple, soft pink, and creamy white, their ruffled petals catching the late afternoon light. Sarah would often sit on the old wooden bench nearby, watching bees drift lazily from bloom to bloom, and think about how her grandmother used to say that gillyflowers carried memories in their fragrance.

This year, Sarah decided to press some of the blossoms between the pages of her grandmother's worn recipe book, hoping to preserve a piece of the garden through the coming winter. As she worked carefully, snipping stems and arranging petals just so, she felt a familiar sense of peace settle over her.

The gillyflowers would fade eventually, as all flowers do, but Sarah found comfort in knowing that next spring, new shoots would emerge from the same soil, carrying forward a tradition that connected her to those who came before. In tending this small patch of garden, she tended something larger too—a thread of continuity stretching back through generations, blooming anew each year in shades of purple and pink and white.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal short poem dedicated to a child named Sarah, "for when she's older," featuring a sad-eyed man who smokes cigars and speaks in riddles.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Sarah, To Be Opened Later

There is a man who lives in the space
between two ticks of a clock,
sad-eyed as a rained-on Sunday,
who smokes cigars that never shrink,
their smoke spelling words backward
in a language only mirrors speak.

He sits on the edge of your future, Sarah,
legs dangling into Tuesday,
and when you're old enough to find him
he'll tilt his hat of graying feathers
and say: *The door is loudest
when nobody knocks.*

You'll ask him what he means.
He'll blow a smoke-ring shaped like your childhood
and say: *The answer was the question's shadow—
follow it before the sun goes down
inside your chest.*

Don't be afraid of his sadness.
It's just weather passing through a borrowed face.
He's been waiting longer than your name existed,
holding this riddle like a coin
warm from someone else's pocket:

*What grows smaller the more you give it away,
yet fills the room when you keep it silent?*

Tell him: *love, or maybe time,
or maybe just the space
where a girl named Sarah
used to be small enough
to not need answers.*

He'll smile then—finally—
ash falling like gray snow
that melts before it lands,
and disappear the way smoke does:
not gone, just elsewhere,
waiting in another Sunday,
another Tuesday,
another version of you
old enough, at last,
to ask him nothing
and understand everything.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you generate a dreamlike piece of flash fiction inspired by a strange painting—something with a round, sad-eyed man, flowers, and a hidden box—written as a keepsake for a daughter?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Keeper of Small Weathers

For my daughter, who asked what the painting meant

In the painting, the round man sits where the garden ends and the wallpaper begins—one leg in the grass, one leg dissolving into a pattern of faded gold fleurs-de-lis. His eyes are the color of rain remembered rather than rain falling. He has always looked this way. He will always look this way. Sadness, on him, is not a weather but a season, patient and entire.

Around his feet: flowers that don't exist in botany books. Blooms like small blue trumpets that seem to be listening. Petals with the particular droop of things that bloomed specifically to keep him company, knowing already how the story ends.

You asked me once what he was so sad about.

I said: *he's not sad about anything. He's sad the way a bell is round.* It's simply the shape he came in.

But here is what I never told you, because you were young and the truth needed to ripen first, like a fruit that isn't sweet until it's nearly too soft to eat:

Underneath him—if you could lift him gently as a lid—there is a box. You cannot see it in the painting. I only know because I dreamed it, three nights running, the autumn before you were born. Small, wooden, the color of an old piano key. Inside: not treasure. Not answers. Just a single flower, pressed flat, and a note in handwriting that isn't mine or his but something older, something that belongs to whoever waters gardens that don't exist.

The note says: *You were loved before the sadness. You will be loved after.*

I think the round man sits atop the box not to hide it, but to keep it warm. I think he has been sitting there so long he's forgotten there's a door beneath him at all—he only remembers the *weight* of guarding something precious, the way you might forget the words to a song but still hum its shape.

Daughter, if you ever feel like the round man—heavy with a sadness that has no edges, no name, no ending—remember: you might be sitting on a box of flowers. You might be the door and the guardian both.

Someday lift yourself gently.

See what's been kept warm underneath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a whimsical, slightly melancholic prose poem that reads like a fairy tale fragment, involving a man who has locked his head in a Japanese box and lost the key. Include a dedication line at the top.
counterfactuals.output:
*for the ones who keep their softness locked away*

Once there was a man who loved his own thoughts so much he built them a house. He found a craftsman in a town that smelled of cedar shavings and rain, and asked for a box with no visible seams, the kind that opens only if you remember the sequence — press here, slide there, turn the moon-shaped panel twice to the left. The craftsman warned him: *some boxes forget how to be opened, if you are not careful.* The man laughed, the way people laugh at warnings meant for other people.

He put his head inside on a Tuesday, if Tuesdays existed where he lived, which is uncertain. He wanted a night's rest from the noise of his own wanting. He wanted to keep his sadness somewhere tidy, labeled, drawered. Click, click, went the panels. The box hummed once, like a cat deciding whether to trust you, and then it was quiet.

He has been quiet ever since.

His wife — if he had one, and I think he did, she had flour always on her sleeves — searched the house for the key. She searched the garden, under stones shaped like sleeping animals. She asked the moon, who is a terrible gossip but useless with facts. She asked the cranes that nest in the eaves each spring, and they only tilted their heads, embarrassed for her.

Seasons did what seasons do. Moss crept along the box's corners like green forgetting. Once, a child pressed an ear to its lacquered side and swore she heard someone humming a lullaby to himself, off-key, patient, as though rehearsing for a performance no one had scheduled.

Some nights the wife sets his chair at the table anyway. She talks to the box about small things — the price of rice, a neighbor's new dog, the particular gray of the sky before snow. She has stopped asking it to open. She has started asking it to *listen,* which it does, beautifully, being a box, having nothing else to do with its evenings.

They say if you find the key you must not use it right away. You must sit with it in your palm first, and ask yourself honestly whether you are ready to see what a person looks like after so long spent folded inside his own keeping.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write something in the style of a surrealist bedtime story, mixing imagery of gillyflowers, purple bells, and an apple on a hill, with a talking figure who seems both alive and not alive.
counterfactuals.output:
The Hill That Remembered Its Own Name

There was, once, a hill so gentle that sheep mistook it for sleep itself, and on this hill grew a single apple, red as a held breath, hanging from a tree that had no other fruit and no particular opinion about being a tree at all.

Around its roots, gillyflowers leaned together like gossiping aunts, their petals the color of old wine and older secrets, whispering to the purple bells that grew between them — the kind of bells that make a sound only when no one is listening, a sound like a name being almost remembered.

*Ding,* went the bells. *Ding, ding.* Not quite music. More like punctuation for the wind.

At the base of the hill sat a figure made of things that should not sit: twigs for elbows, a lantern for a head, a coat stitched from the same purple as the bells, as though it had grown up out of the ground alongside them rather than been placed there by any hand. It rocked slightly, the way old porches rock, though there was no wind strong enough to move it.

"Are you sleeping?" asked the figure, to no one, or perhaps to the apple.

The apple did not answer, because apples generally don't, but the figure waited anyway, patient as a held door.

"I was alive once," it said. "Or I will be. I can never remember which direction I'm facing in time. It's like standing in a hallway with no doors, only the memory of doors, only the smell of a house that hasn't been built."

The gillyflowers rustled their agreement. The bells rang their small, purple ring.

"The apple up there," the figure continued, gesturing with an elbow that clicked like a clock deciding not to strike, "is either a beginning or an ending. I've asked it. It only hangs there, being red, being a held breath, being extremely polite about not falling."

A gillyflower unfurled slightly, as if to speak, then thought better of it and simply deepened its color instead.

"Someday," said the figure, "someone will climb this hill in a nightgown the color of not-quite-morning, and they will pick the apple, and the bells will ring so hard they'll wake the sheep who are pretending to be the hill, and the hill will remember its own name for just one moment — long enough to sigh — and then forget again, the way all soft things do."

The lantern-head flickered, though there was no flame in it, only the idea of one.

"But that is not tonight," the figure said, settling back into its rocking, which was not quite rocking, into its sitting, which was not quite stillness. "Tonight the apple stays red. Tonight the bells keep their secret. Tonight you are almost asleep, and I am almost here, and that is enough — that is always, somehow, enough."

The purple bells rang once more, so softly it might have been imagined, and the hill — pretending to be a hill, the way it always did — breathed out, and the dreaming began.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short, poetic narrative addressed to a young girl named Sarah, filled with strange symbolic imagery (cigars, locked heads, flowers) that blurs the line between memory, loss, and imagination.
counterfactuals.output:
# For Sarah, Who Asked What I Remember

Sarah, there was a house that smoked like an old man's cigar,
ash falling soft as September onto the porch where you learned to walk.
Your grandfather's mouth was a locked door
and inside it, a key made of smoke,
and inside the smoke, a garden nobody planted.

I remember flowers that grew backwards—
petals folding into seed, into dirt, into the hand that never held them.
You were three. You thought the marigolds were talking.
Maybe they were. Maybe everything speaks
if you're small enough to hear it.

There is a room in me shaped like your first birthday,
and the door has seven locks
and I have lost six of the keys
and the seventh opens onto nothing—
just more doors, smaller,
like a cigar box full of cigar boxes,
each one holding a single spark
that refuses to become fire or ash,
just stays there, glowing,
patient as a held breath.

Sarah, your head is not locked, not yet.
It's a field still. Let it be a field.
Let the flowers grow whichever way they please—
forward into fruit, backward into wonder,
sideways into the strange logic of five-year-old Tuesdays.

I don't remember everything.
I remember the shape memory leaves
when it burns down to filter,
when it curls like paper going soft with rain,
when it becomes the smell that means *before*—

before you knew doors could lock,
before flowers seemed like something
other than miracles,
before I learned to smoke my grief
instead of speaking it.

Here. Take the last of the matches.
Light something small.
Not to remember—
to see what's still here,
still yours,
still growing the right way up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
